title: If Private Equity Can't Model Five Years Out, How Can a Sixteen-Year-Old?
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard uses an Axios report on AI's disruption of private equity modeling as a lens to expose the structural absurdity of asking high school juniors to choose college majors. PE firms with armies of analysts and direct AI-lab relationships openly admit they cannot model portfolio value across a four-to-seven-year hold period because AI makes economic outcomes un-modelable; yet the American education system asks sixteen-year-olds to make a more confident five-to-six-year forecast about labor market value. The comparison is asymmetric in every way: a PE firm holds twenty-plus companies and can write down losses, while the student bets on one major with potentially six figures of debt and no diversification. The advice infrastructure students rely on — guidance counselors, salary-projection websites, parents drawing on forty years of career stability — is calibrated to historical patterns that no longer hold, with the occupations most confidently recommended (accounting, law, medicine, software development) precisely those AI is currently disrupting most aggressively. The education system's structural inertia — tenure, accreditation cycles, four-year program requirements — means it will take fifteen to twenty years to reckon with credential devaluation that capital markets absorb in five to ten, leaving students currently in high school making decisions inside a framework that cannot adjust in time. Bauschard's prescription is not to skip college but to replace the 'major-as-forecast' model with education built around AI-resilient capacities: real-time reasoning, adversarial argumentation, evidence evaluation, and ethical judgment under pressure — domain-independent capacities that survive any configuration of the labor market.
points: The most sophisticated capital allocators on earth — PE firms with dedicated AI analysts and institutional resources — openly tell the financial press that three-to-four-year investment horizons are now un-modelable; asking high school students to make longer-horizon career forecasts without those resources is structurally incoherent.

The asymmetry of consequences is extreme: when PE gets the model wrong, diversified institutional limited partners absorb losses across a portfolio; when a student gets the bet wrong, there is one life, four years, opportunity cost, and debt that follows for decades.

Education's institutional structure (tenure, accreditation, four-year programs) will require fifteen to twenty years to reckon with credential devaluation that capital markets absorb in five to ten — students currently in high school will make decisions inside a framework that cannot adjust in time to help them.

The capacities Bauschard identifies as AI-resilient — real-time reasoning under pressure, adversarial argumentation, evidence evaluation, ethical judgment, dialogue across genuine disagreement — are domain-independent and valuable in any possible economic configuration, unlike specific knowledge bundles tied to particular industries.

Speech and debate — the most direct institutional training ground for these AI-resilient capacities — is funded as an extracurricular club while resources flow to coursework preparing students for careers that may not exist upon graduation.
quotes: The most sophisticated capital allocators on earth—people who employ armies of analysts, who can pay for any consultant, who have direct relationships with the AI labs themselves—are openly admitting they cannot model what the world looks like in 4 years.
We are asking sixteen-year-olds to make a more confident forecast about the labor market than Blackstone is willing to make about its own portfolio.

When a student gets the bet wrong, there is no portfolio. There is one life, four years, the opportunity cost of those years, and—often—debt that follows them for decades. The 'exit multiple' they're trying to model is their own first job.
The advice sounds prudent. The advice may be catastrophic. And the people giving it have no way to know which.

The educational system refuses to admit it doesn't know. Walk into almost any high school in America, and you'll find the same machinery still running: course catalogs organized around traditional career pathways, guidance counselors steering students toward 'stable' professions, AP tracks designed to feed pre-med and pre-law and pre-business pipelines.
We are sending them toward destinations that may not exist when they arrive, and the system is pretending otherwise.

A student who can think well, evaluate evidence, and defend ideas under cross-examination has a portable capacity that survives any specific economic configuration. A student who has memorized the 2026 marketing curriculum does not.
We are lowballing the only thing we know is durable, while we keep dressing up the things we don't know in the costume of certainty.
